outcome: No characterization of the number fields that have a power integral basis has appeared since 26 January 2024. The window adds monogenic polynomial families, criteria for pure, radical, composed and polynomial-defined families, a 2024 construction-and-density set of results, and a June 2026 preprint giving infinitely many non-monogenic fields in every degree above 2; none of these settles the problem as stated, which remains open. No AI system is credited with any result on this problem.
problem_asks: Reading adopted (judging pass to confirm): the statement's words say 'power basis'. Every number field K of degree n has a power basis over Q, namely 1, a, a^2, ..., a^(n-1) for a primitive element a (primitive element theorem), so read literally the problem is already satisfied by every field. The problem as Wikipedia's link target and the literature (Hasse's problem) use it is therefore a power integral basis: O_K = Z[theta] for some theta in O_K, i.e. K is monogenic. Parts: (1) for each algebraic number field K, decide whether O_K has a power integral basis; (2) characterize the class of fields for which it does, by an arithmetic/explicit criterion ('characterize all'); (3) the criterion must cover all degrees n >= 2 (the statement names no degree restriction), not only particular families or degrees. Equivalent index-form formulation: K is monogenic iff the index form of K takes the value +1 or -1 on the integer points of its lattice. Degrees 1 and 2 are trivially monogenic; the first non-monogenic field (Dedekind, cubic) shows the class is proper.

events.what_happened: Dedekind’s cubic field generated by a root of x^3 - x^2 - 2x - 8 is not monogenic: the prime 2 splits completely in it, and a monic cubic cannot split completely mod 2 into distinct linear factors with the needed property, so no theta generates O_K. Recorded as the classical first non-monogenic example; not opened in primary form (see incomplete).
events.delivers: Shows that not every cubic field (indeed not every field of degree >= 3) is monogenic; the class is proper. Restriction: one specific field.
events.remains: Every other field; a characterization of the monogenic class.
events.directly_checkable: Checkable by hand: 2 splits completely in the field, and the argument modulo 2 shows no generator with the required factorization. Secondary sources (search snippets) agree on the argument and the polynomial, with one source giving x^3 + x^2 - 2x + 8 (a sign variant) that I treat as a transcription variant.
events.doubts: Only secondary sources for the 1878 publication were seen; the primary Göttingen paper was not opened, and one search snippet dates an example to 1871 in another text. The 1878 date is the standard attribution.
events.direction: Negative: this field admits no power integral basis, so the answer to 'which fields are monogenic' is not 'all fields'.
events.object: The cubic field generated by a root of x^3 - x^2 - 2x - 8, with 2 split completely; non-monogenic by a local argument mod 2 (the field is the object, the non-existence of a generator is the claim).

events.what_happened: Jakhar, Kalwaniya and Yadav, 'Monogenic Fields from Polynomial Compositions with Applications', arXiv 2605.00949 (v1 1 May 2026). Necessary and sufficient conditions for index-one monogenity of fields generated by roots of composed polynomials f_i(x^k + b), i = 1, 2; asymptotic counts of monogenic polynomials under assumptions; a class of polynomials with non-square-free discriminant.
events.delivers: Explicit monogenity criteria for two composed polynomial families (polynomial-level conditions; field-level consequence for those fields). Restricted to those families; asymptotic counts are conditional on 'natural assumptions'.
events.remains: General characterization; the assumptions behind the counting estimates are not verified here.
events.doubts: Abstract only read; the counting estimates are conditional.
events.direction: Positive but restricted: criteria for specific composed families.

events.what_happened: Barman, Jakhar, Kalwaniya and Yadav, 'Arithmetic Aspects of Number Fields Generated by Polynomial Families', arXiv 2602.19726 (v1 23 Feb 2026). For f(x) = (x^k + c)^m − a x^n, km > n: explicit discriminant formula; necessary and sufficient conditions for monogenity in terms of prime divisors of a and c and k, m, n; infinite families of monogenic polynomials of arbitrary degree, some with non-square-free discriminant; extension to g(f(x)) for arbitrary g; field-index conditions giving partial progress on a problem of Narkiewicz.
events.delivers: Necessary and sufficient monogenity conditions for the explicit family (x^k + c)^m − a x^n; composite extension with explicit but unquoted conditions. Restricted to that polynomial family and its composites.
events.remains: General characterization of monogenic fields; other polynomial families; the field-index valuations for all primes (only sufficient conditions given).
events.directly_checkable: Explicit discriminant formula and index conditions are checkable on specific a, c, k, m, n (not read).
events.doubts: Abstract only read.
events.direction: Positive but restricted: monogenity criteria for an explicit polynomial family.

events.what_happened: Sharma and Sarma, 'Monogenity of the composition of certain polynomials', Acta Arithmetica 222 (2026), 265–277, DOI 10.4064/aa250626-9-9, published online 18 Jan 2026 (publisher page). Establishes a necessary condition for monogenity of a composition of two polynomials; characterizes certain primes dividing the index of f(x^m + a) when irreducible; gives a sufficient condition for monogenity of f(x^m + a) and a new infinite family of monogenic polynomials. No arXiv version was found; the publisher page was opened.
events.revisions: Online publication 18 Jan 2026 (publisher); a 17.01.2026 date appears on a mirror. No earlier preprint found.
events.delivers: A necessary condition for monogenity of composed polynomials, and a sufficient condition for f(x^m + a) with an infinite family of monogenic polynomials. Restricted to compositions; polynomial-level.
events.remains: A general characterization of monogenic fields; the sufficiency condition is not necessary in general.
events.direction: Positive but restricted: a necessary condition and a sufficient condition for composed polynomials.

events.what_happened: Nguyen-Dang, 'Eisenstein-prime Obstruction Sieve for Monogenicity', arXiv 2602.10488 (v1 11 Feb 2026, only version; 31 pages). For pure fields K_m = Q(alpha), alpha^n = m, n ≥ 4, m square-free: the set of m for which the index g(m) > 1 but K_m has no ABS local obstruction has natural density 0; so monogenicity and alpha-monogenicity have the same density in the pure family. Introduces an 'Eisenstein-prime obstruction sieve' template. The abstract restates that ABS showed a positive proportion of cubic and quartic fields are non-monogenic despite the fixed-sign local condition.
events.delivers: A density-zero statement inside the pure family K_m (n ≥ 4, m square-free): among square-free m, non-monogenic pure fields without an ABS local obstruction are density zero. Restricted to pure fields with square-free m. It is a statement about density within a family, not a characterization of monogenic fields.
events.remains: A characterization of monogenic fields in the pure family or in general; non-square-free m; non-pure families (the author says the argument 'transfers' to other Eisenstein families as a template only).
events.doubts: The full text was not readable (compressed PDF), so the proof and the acknowledgements were not checked. Abstract only.
events.direction: Partial: a density result for a pure family; cuts neither way on the characterization.

sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10488 (abstract page; no AI mention). Full PDF fetched but unreadable, so acknowledgements were NOT checked.

events.what_happened: Choudhary, Pisolkar and Yadav, 'Power Integral Bases in Polynomial Compositions', arXiv 2606.09739 (v1 8 Jun 2026). For composed polynomials (f o g)(x) with f = x^n + a x^(n-1) + d x^(n-2) + b (a^2 = 4d) and g = x^m + c, assuming irreducibility: necessary and sufficient conditions on a, b, c, d, m, n for monogenity; lower bound on the count of such polynomials; non-square-free discriminant examples.
events.delivers: Necessary and sufficient monogenity conditions for a specific composed family under an irreducibility hypothesis. Restricted to that family.
events.remains: General characterization; composed families other than this one.
events.doubts: Abstract only read; the explicit conditions not visible.
events.direction: Positive but restricted to a composed family.

events.what_happened: Gaál, 'Monogenity of pure quintic fields: the power of sieving', arXiv 2605.03392 (v1 5 May 2026; v2 11 May 2026). Gives a simple algorithm for calculating all generators of power integral bases in pure quintic fields, using Baker's method and LLL-reduction plus a sieve that tests the remaining small exponents 'within a few minutes'.
events.delivers: Per the abstract, an algorithm that computes all generators of power integral bases for pure quintic fields. Restricted to pure quintic fields; whether it decides monogenity for every pure quintic field (not only computes generators) is not stated in the abstract.
events.remains: A closed-form characterization of monogenic pure quintic fields; monogenity of non-pure quintic fields; degrees other than 5.
events.directly_checkable: Algorithmic outputs for given pure quintic fields (not read).
events.doubts: Abstract only read; the sieve step's completeness argument not visible.
events.direction: Computational, restricted to pure quintic fields; cuts neither way on the characterization of all fields.

events.what_happened: Hanson Smith, 'Number Fields with Arbitrarily Large Minimal Index', arXiv 2606.25841 (v1 24 Jun 2026, only version). Defines the minimal index of K as the least positive m such that some monogenic order has index m in the maximal order. For every n > 2 and N > 1, constructs infinitely many number fields of degree n with minimal index greater than N. Since minimal index > 1 forces non-monogenicity, this gives infinitely many non-monogenic fields in every degree n > 2.
events.delivers: For every degree n > 2: infinitely many fields of degree n that are not monogenic (indeed with minimal index > N for any given N). Restricted to degrees n > 2; says nothing about which fields are monogenic, and nothing about degrees 1 and 2 (which are trivially monogenic).
events.remains: A characterization of which fields are monogenic; whether the monogenic fields of a given degree are finite, zero-density, or infinite in number; the proportion question.
events.directly_checkable: The construction is of explicit fields (degree-n fields built by a construction in the paper); a specific example was not read.
events.doubts: Abstract page read; the PDF body was compressed and unreadable, so the proof, the introduction’s account of the monogenity problem, and the acknowledgements were not checked. Degrees, method and the construction were not visible.
events.direction: Negative in the sense of the complement: infinitely many non-monogenic fields in every degree above 2; does not cut the characterization either way.
events.object: Infinite families of degree-n number fields (n > 2) whose minimal index exceeds any given N; each such field is not monogenic. Construction type (explicit or not) not visible from the abstract.

sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25841 (abstract page; no AI mention). The PDF was fetched but unreadable; acknowledgements NOT checked.

events.what_happened: Adhikari, Plott and Torgersen, 'Monogenic Fields of Cryptographic Size', arXiv 2609.22374 (v1 17 Sep 2026, only version). For monic irreducible f of degree n and integer c, the palindromic transform F(x) = x^n f(x + x^(-1) + c) (degree 2n): discriminant formula disc(F) = f(c+2) f(c-2) disc(f)^2; a criterion that F is monogenic when f is monogenic and f(c+2)f(c-2) is square-free, with a matching non-monogenicity criterion; iterating yields monogenic fields of degree 2^k n; explicit monogenic field of degree 512 from x^4 + x + 1.
events.delivers: Constructs monogenic fields of degrees 2^k n from a monogenic base polynomial, with a monogenicity criterion for the transform (a sufficient and matching non-sufficient criterion, per the abstract). Restricted to the palindromic-transform family; constructive existence, not characterization.
events.remains: A characterization of monogenic fields; monogenicity of fields outside the transform family; the degree-2n conjecture reported by a search summary is not in the abstract (see doubts).
events.directly_checkable: The degree-512 example is a specific polynomial-generated field, checkable by discriminant and index computation (not run).
events.doubts: A search summary attributed to this paper a conjecture about infinitely many monogenic fields of degree 2n; the abstract page I opened states no such conjecture. I treat the summary as wrong on this point. Abstract only; the full text was not readable in this run. Too recent for any review.
events.direction: Positive (existence): monogenic fields of degrees 2^k n; not a characterization.
events.object: Monogenic field of degree 512 obtained by iterating the palindromic transform from the base polynomial x^4 + x + 1; explicit, constructive. Its monogenicity is claimed via the paper’s criterion.

summary: Nothing since 26 January 2024 settles this problem as stated. The problem, read as the literature reads it (Hasse’s problem: O_K = Z[theta]), asks for an arithmetic characterization of all monogenic number fields in all degrees. The literal reading (K = Q(alpha) with 1, alpha, ..., alpha^(n-1) a Q-basis) is satisfied by every field by the primitive element theorem; I record that reading and adopt the power-integral-basis one, and the judging pass should confirm it. The Wikipedia bullet, verified verbatim in the list’s 'Algebraic number theory' section, reads: 'Characterize all algebraic number fields that have some power basis.' It links to 'Algebraic number field' (its 'Bases for number fields' subsection), which I did not read. The window’s work is substantial but restricted. It includes monogenic polynomial families and their Galois groups (Harrington–Jones 2024, Jones 2025, Barman et al. 2026, Choudhary et al. 2026, Jakhar et al. 2026, Sharma–Sarma 2026); generator-computation algorithms for named families of fields (Gaál 2024–2026: quartic, octic, sextic with quadratic subfield, pure quintic); local-obstruction and splitting results for radical fields (Smith 2024, Scofield–Smith 2025); density and proportion statements (Nguyen-Dang 2026; Alpöge–Bhargava–Shnidman 2020–21, the last two being pre-window); a 2026 construction giving monogenic fields of degree 2^k n (Adhikari et al., September 2026); and, most consequentially for the 'does it move' question, Smith’s 24 June 2026 preprint giving infinitely many non-monogenic fields in every degree n > 2. None of these characterizes monogenic fields in any degree. The closest-to-settling in-window claim is Andrade–Facini–Esteves (BSPM, 14 Feb 2025), which a search snippet describes as a 'complete answer' to Hasse’s problem for pure quintic fields; the journal abstract I opened concerns integral bases, and the introduction was not visible, so the scope is unverified. Gaál’s 5 May 2026 preprint gives an algorithm for all generators in pure quintic fields; whether that decides monogenity for every pure quintic field is not stated in the abstract. Pre-window classical results carry the substance of the characterizations so far: Gaál and Remete (2017) for pure fields of degrees 3–9 with square-free m, with an almost complete characterization for degrees 4, 6, 8; Kashio and Sekigawa (arXiv December 2019) for cyclic cubic fields, reducing monogenic ones to simplest cubic fields with an explicit criterion; Nyul (2001) for mixed-sign biquadratic fields, reducing monogenity to a solvable index-form equation. Two checks: (i) for every event, the sources I read were abstract pages; where I could not read a PDF body (Smith 2606.25841, Nguyen-Dang 2602.10488, Nyul 2001, Alpöge–Bhargava–Shnidman cubic v1), acknowledgements and theorem statements are unchecked; (ii) the AI search (§4) found no system credited with any result on monogenic fields, power integral bases or the index form in any source. The only AI-credited result in the window touching number fields is OpenAI’s May 2026 unit-distance counterexample (companion arXiv 2605.20695), which uses class-field-tower ideas for a geometric problem and is recorded as discarded for this problem. Quanta, Terence Tao, and Lean/mathlib searches found no monogenicity result; the Erdős Problems database search found no number-field power-basis entry. Close calls: (a) whether Smith’s 2026 'infinitely many non-monogenic fields in each degree n > 2' moves the problem: it gives no characterization, but it fixes the complement of the monogenic class in every degree above 2 and so is the strongest in-window statement about which fields are not monogenic; (b) whether the Scofield–Smith and Smith (2024, 2025) local-obstruction papers move the problem: they classify obstructions for radical fields and exhibit non-monogenic fields without common index divisors, so they bear on the proof technique rather than the characterization; (c) whether the Jones and Harrington–Jones families count: they establish infinitely many monogenic fields in named families, which is an existence result within a class, not a characterization. Discrepancies noted: a search summary attributed to Adhikari et al. a conjecture on degree 2n monogenic fields that the abstract does not contain; the Andrade et al. claim above; a search summary gave a Dedekind polynomial with a sign variant, treated as transcription. A Shnidman folklore conjecture (monogenic proportion zero for each degree d > 2, from a 2023 slide deck) was seen only in a search snippet and is not recorded as an event; it is a conjecture, not a result, and the slide deck was not opened. The Stanford 'UQ' pages and an AI-generated answer state that whether every number field embeds in a monogenic one is open; that is a different problem and not recorded. Narkiewicz Problem 22 (explicit power of a prime dividing the field index) and Engstrom’s 1930 degree-<8 index results are neighbouring and are mentioned here but not recorded as events.
competing_reading: (1) Read the 2026 results as moving the problem: Smith (24 June 2026) gives infinitely many non-monogenic fields in every degree n > 2, and Scofield–Smith gives non-monogenic fields that evade all common index divisors. A judging pass could count these as progress toward the characterization because they settle the non-monogenic side in every degree above 2 (not for a specific field, but in quantity). Against this: the problem asks for a criterion that decides each field, and infinitely many non-monogenic fields in each degree is a statement about density/abundance, which does not decide any specific field. (2) Read Andrade–Facini–Esteves (2025) as a complete answer for pure quintic fields: this would settle the problem for one family (pure quintic fields) if the introduction's claim is about power integral bases. Against: the opened abstract is about integral bases, and Gaál's 2026 work on pure quintic fields still treats generators as open. (3) Read Gaál’s 2026 pure-quintic algorithm as a decision procedure for every pure quintic field, which would be a characterization for one family. Against: the abstract claims computation of all generators, not a proof that every pure quintic field is covered by the sieve; the completeness argument is not visible. (4) Read the Reading 2 literal sense of 'power basis' as the problem's meaning; on that reading every field satisfies it and the problem has no open content. This is a reading the judging pass should be able to reject explicitly, and I have not treated it as the intended one.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The introduction and main theorem of Andrade–Facini–Esteves, BSPM 43 (2025), to see whether the claimed complete answer concerns power integral bases for pure quintic fields. (b) The full text of Gaál arXiv 2605.03392 to see whether the algorithm decides monogenity for every pure quintic field (and whether its sieve is complete). (c) The readable PDF bodies of Smith arXiv 2606.25841 (degrees, construction, and acknowledgements) and Nguyen-Dang arXiv 2602.10488 (proof and acknowledgements). (d) The text of Gaál’s 2024 survey open-problems section (arXiv 2407.00374, section 4), verbatim, to see whether it poses the general Hasse problem as open. (e) Gras (1973) and the Dedekind (1878) primary sources, which are not opened here. (f) The Alpöge–Bhargava–Shnidman journal versions (Mathematische Annalen), to verify the Springer details, which were not retrieved. (g) The full list of counterexamples in Sra’s 'GPT, the Counterexample Machine' (arXiv 2608.29595), to see whether any concerns monogenicity; the abstract does not list them. (h) A search of arXiv monogenic/power-integral-basis listings for 2026 (the listing pages were not browsed; coverage here is by web search), to test whether a general characterization has appeared and was missed.
